Female Ocean pout attain a maximum total length of 110 cm [Li = 110 cm], making them the largest members of the family Zoarcidae in the western North Atlantic. Field surveys along the continental shelf from Nova Scotia to Cape Cod indicate that this ultimate size is reached gradually over many years. Maturation, however, occurs at a considerably smaller body size; the total length at puberty for female individuals has been documented at 28.8 cm [Lp = 28.8 cm], a threshold that signals the onset of gonadal recrudescence and vitellogenesis. The corresponding body mass at this developmental stage is approximately 87 grams [Wwp = approximately 87 grams], reflecting the moderate condition of sub-adult fish prior to their first investment in egg production. This relatively low mass at sexual maturity, compared to the enormous potential size of fully grown females, underscores the strongly indeterminate growth pattern characteristic of this cold-water benthic species.

Newly hatched Ocean pout emerge from demersal, adhesive eggs as well-developed yolk-sac larvae. The embryonic incubation period is surprisingly protracted under the cold conditions typical of the species' native habitat; at a stable temperature of 3 °C [T = 3 °C], eclosion occurs after approximately 84 days [ab = approximately 84 days]. This duration corresponds to roughly two to three months of yolk-dependent development within the chorion, a slow pace consistent with the low metabolic rates imposed by near-freezing bottom water temperatures. At the moment of hatching, the prolarvae carry a modest wet weight at birth of 0.0654 grams [Wwb = 0.0654 grams], a value that aligns closely with the theoretical mass predicted from an average egg diameter of 5 millimeters. This small initial size places the newly emerged larvae in a highly endotrophic phase, relying entirely on their yolk reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding.

The reproductive output of large, mature Ocean pout females is substantial. At a body length of approximately 62 centimeters, females maintained under a controlled thermal regime of 3 °C [T = 3 °C] produce roughly 1805 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = roughly 1805 eggs per spawning event], and they typically spawn once per year [F_R_i = spawn once per year]. This annual reproductive schedule is characteristic of many iteroparous boreal fishes that experience a single, well-defined spawning season. The ultimate wet weight for female Ocean pout can reach approximately 6300 grams [Wwi = approximately 6300 grams], a value derived from established length-weight relationships for the species. Achieving such a massive adult body size allows older females to generate these large clutches, a classic example of the fecundity advantages conferred by indeterminate growth in teleost fishes.

Longevity in Ocean pout is considerable for a fish of its thermal environment. Under the sustained cold conditions of 3 °C [T = 3 °C], the maximum lifespan for this species has been recorded at approximately 19 years [am = approximately 19 years]. This extended lifespan is consistent with the observation that growth continues throughout most of the adult life, with the largest females accumulating body mass and length over many decades. The oldest documented individuals, collected from trawl surveys in the Gulf of Maine, show little evidence of reproductive senescence, continuing to produce large clutches of demersal eggs well into their second decade. When compared to other zoarcids inhabiting similar thermal niches, the maximum longevity of Ocean pout falls at the higher end of the range, reflecting a life-history strategy that prioritizes repeated spawning events and prolonged somatic growth over rapid, early reproduction.

The large ultimate size and delayed maturation of female Ocean pout have notable implications for population resilience, particularly in the context of commercial bycatch pressure. Compared to other boreal zoarcids such as Lycodes reticulatus, which matures earlier and at smaller sizes, Ocean pout channel a greater proportion of somatic growth into body length before diverting resources toward reproduction, a strategy that buffers against year-to-year variability in prey availability. The combination of protracted embryonic development, modest annual fecundity of roughly 1805 demersal eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = roughly 1805 demersal eggs per spawning event], and repeated spawning over a lifespan that can exceed two decades produces a slow demographic turnover typical of species adapted to stable, cold environments. This life-history syndrome renders the species more vulnerable to sustained removal rates, as recovery from population declines would necessarily involve prolonged rebuilding of the adult stock.
